**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two of our internal tools have started timing out intermittently. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy more GPUs or squeeze more out of the fleet we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this trade-off, because the right answer is less obvious than it appears, and I'd like us to make the decision deliberately rather than by default.

The case for buying hardware is straightforward: our utilization numbers during business hours are genuinely high, and the pain is real. Latency is not a cosmetic problem for us. When a developer waits ninety seconds for a completion, they context-switch, and the quietly stops being part of their workflow. Every minute of queue time is a small tax on the whole team's attention, multiplied across dozens of users a day. New hardware would make that tax disappear almost immediately, and it would give us headroom for the model upgrades we know are coming, which tend to be larger and hungrier than what they replace.

But the case for improving utilization first is stronger than it might look, for reasons that have less to do with the purchase price and more to do with what we'd be locking in. GPUs depreciate quickly and resell poorly; a purchase made to solve a peak-hour problem is a purchase we own through every trough. Right now our utilization profile is spiky — near saturation midday, largely idle overnight and on weekends. That shape suggests we may not have a capacity problem so much as a scheduling and efficiency problem. Batched inference, better request coalescing, quantized models for workloads that don't need full precision, and moving long-running batch jobs to off-peak windows could plausibly recover twenty to thirty percent of effective capacity at a cost of a few engineering weeks. That is a very different price tag from a capital purchase, and it's one we can afford to be wrong about.

There's also the question of what we'd give up. The capital we'd spend on hardware is capital not spent on the roadmap work that's actually differentiated for us. Nobody remembers us for owning more GPUs; they remember us for shipping. And hardware purchases are, in a meaningful sense, the least reversible decision available to us. Model versions can be rolled back, caching layers can be removed, a scheduling change can be reverted in an afternoon. A rack of accelerators is a commitment that outlasts our current understanding of our own demand curve, which — if I'm honest — is built on six weeks of data from a team whose usage patterns are still settling as more people adopt the tools.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to acknowledge that. More hardware means redundancy: if a node dies today, we degrade noticeably, and a second node would soften that. Better utilization, by contrast, often means running closer to the edge, with less slack to absorb failures or traffic spikes. I don't want to optimize ourselves into a system where a single hot job at 2pm takes down the queue for everyone. Any utilization work we do has to preserve a deliberate buffer, and we should treat that buffer as a feature, not waste.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next six to eight weeks on utilization — batching, quantization where quality permits, off-peak scheduling, and honest instrumentation so we can see whether the improvements are real — while simultaneously writing the purchase order for a modest hardware addition and holding it, unsigned, pending the results. If utilization work gets peak queue times back under a few seconds, we cancel the order and bank the savings. If it doesn't, we will have learned a great deal about our actual demand shape, and we'll buy with better information, likely needing less than we think today. This path is reversible at every step, defers irreversible spending until we've earned confidence, and costs us only engineering time we'd probably spend firefighting anyway.

The main uncertainty I'd flag is that utilization gains are estimates until measured, and our demand may grow faster than we can optimize. If peak load jumps again mid-quarter, we should treat that as evidence and accelerate the purchase rather than defend the plan. The goal is a decision process, not a decision made once and defended forever.

Happy to discuss on Thursday.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Recommendation in brief:** We should spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases, while keeping a purchase option warm so we can execute quickly if utilisation work stalls or demand surprises us.

**Context**

We currently operate eight A100-class GPUs across two nodes, and our internal telemetry tells an uncomfortable story: average utilisation sits around 35–40%, with peak bursts to 90% during batch inference windows and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. At the same time, several teams are queuing for capacity, and the frustration is real. The instinctive response — buy more — is understandable, but buying hardware to serve demand we cannot currently schedule efficiently is like hiring more staff before fixing a broken shift roster. The cheapest GPU is the one we already own.

**The economics**

A new node of comparable capability would cost roughly $180–220K upfront, plus meaningful increases in power, cooling, colocation, and the engineering time to integrate and operate it. Depreciation aside, the true cost includes the opportunity cost of that capital: the same money could fund two additional engineers for a year, and headcount is arguably our scarcer resource. Meanwhile, our utilisation problem is largely a scheduling and fragmentation problem. Jobs are pinned to specific GPUs to avoid contention, long-running notebooks squat on memory they rarely use, and batch workloads run at peak hours alongside interactive traffic. If we lifted average utilisation to 65–70% — an ambitious but achievable target based on what peer teams report — we would effectively add three to four GPUs of capacity for the cost of engineering time we mostly already have.

**Latency and reliability**

Utilisation is not free, and we should be honest about the trade-offs. Consolidating workloads onto a shared scheduler introduces queueing. Interactive and latency-sensitive workloads — the demo endpoints and the human-in-the-loop reviewing — will tolerate some of this, but p99 latency will degrade if we oversubscribe carelessly. Our plan must therefore include workload classes: interactive jobs get guaranteed reservations, batch jobs fill the gaps. This is standard practice, but it is real engineering work, roughly four to six weeks of one engineer's time, and it carries migration risk.

Reliability cuts both ways. Today, our two-node setup means a single node failure removes half our capacity, and our maintenance windows are painful because everything is already tight. A third node would genuinely improve fault tolerance in a way that better scheduling cannot. This is the strongest argument for purchase, and I do not want to minimise it. However, our current failure history — one node incident in eighteen months, recovered in under four hours — suggests our reliability exposure is real but not acute. Better checkpointing and faster failover procedures would buy us most of the resilience at a fraction of the cost.

**Reversibility**

This is where the asymmetry becomes decisive. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible commitment: depreciation, resale friction, and the operational footprint persist regardless of whether demand materialises. Improving utilisation is reversible by design — if our scheduler work underperforms, we have lost weeks, not hundreds of thousands of dollars, and we have gained operational knowledge that makes any eventual purchase smarter. Conversely, if we buy now and utilisation work would have succeeded, we are stuck carrying idle capital for years. When one option preserves optionality and the other destroys it, and both nominally solve the problem, the reversible one deserves the first chance.

**What I propose**

Commit the quarter to the utilisation track: deploy a shared scheduler with workload classes, enforce idle-timeout reclamation on notebooks, shift batch inference to off-peak windows, and publish utilisation dashboards so progress is visible and accountable. Set a decision gate at the end of the quarter: if sustained utilisation exceeds 60% and queue wait times are acceptable, we defer purchase and revisit in six months. If we fall short, or if demand growth outpaces the gains, we proceed to purchase with a well-documented baseline and a scheduler that will make the new hardware work harder from day one.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag two things we do not know. First, our demand forecast is soft; if the new model evaluation programme lands a major customer, capacity needs could double within weeks, and the calculus changes immediately. Second, utilisation gains are notoriously harder to realise than to project — political resistance to giving up pinned GPUs is a real force, and I expect some friction. Both uncertainties argue for the same course: buy time with cheap, reversible work, and keep the purchase decision open rather than foreclosing it now.

I am happy to walk through the numbers in detail at Thursday's planning session.

— Infrastructure Team

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on our compute capacity decision

**Summary**

We recommend spending the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases. The case for buying is real, but it is weaker than it first appears, and the option to buy later does not expire. The option to understand our own fleet better does.

**The situation**

Our four A100 nodes are busy. Scheduling queues have lengthened, researchers are waiting days for slots, and the natural instinct in a room full of impatient engineers is to buy our way out. That instinct deserves respect — but it also deserves scrutiny, because "the queue is long" and "we need more hardware" are not the same claim. The first is an observation. The second is one of several possible explanations, and we have not yet done the work to distinguish it from the alternatives.

**What we actually know**

The strongest argument for purchase is latency. When a training run waits three days to start, iteration slows, and slow iteration has a real cost that is easy to underestimate because it never appears on an invoice. It shows up as delayed experiments, demoralised researchers, and decisions made on stale results. If our utilisation were already high and well-scheduled, this argument would be close to decisive.

But our utilisation is not actually high, or at least we cannot demonstrate that it is. Our best estimates put average GPU utilisation in the 40–55% range, with wide error bars, because our monitoring was built for uptime rather than for understanding how compute is consumed. Anecdotally, we know that jobs are frequently allocated for more memory than they use, that several long-running experiments sit idle over weekends holding their reservations, and that our largest jobs are scheduled first-come-first-served with no preemption. In other words, we may be capacity-constrained, or we may be allocation-constrained, and the remedies differ enormously in cost.

**Cost and opportunity cost**

A new node costs roughly $180k up front plus power, cooling, and — the number nobody budgets — the ongoing engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. **MEMO: Hardware Purchase vs. Utilisation Improvement — Recommendation**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI compute capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?

**Background**

Over the past quarter, our local inference hardware has become the bottleneck for several projects. Queue times for the GPU cluster have grown, two teams have resorted to running jobs overnight, and at least one experiment was quietly abandoned because nobody could get a slot. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy more hardware. The less obvious question — and the one I want to argue is the more important one — is whether we are actually using what we own well enough to know that we need more.

**Where we stand**

Our utilisation numbers are uncomfortable reading. Across the fleet, average GPU utilisation sits around 35–40%, and that figure is flattered by a handful of long-running training jobs. Most requests are bursty: a developer needs a card for twenty minutes, holds it for two hours, and much of that time the silicon is idle. We have no meaningful scheduling layer, no preemption, and no shared queue. Cards are effectively allocated by whoever asks loudest. In other words, we may not have a capacity problem so much as an allocation problem.

**The case for buying**

Buying more hardware has real appeal. It is fast — procurement can have cards on the rack within weeks — and it is politically easy, because nobody has to change how they work. It also buys genuine headroom: if a major experiment lands next quarter, spare capacity is insurance against the kind of schedule slip that costs far more than a GPU. Latency for individual jobs would drop immediately, and reliability would improve in the sense that contention-driven failures and rushed, poorly monitored runs would decline.

**The case against buying — for now**

But the costs are not trivial. Capital outlay for meaningful capacity is substantial, and it is largely irreversible at our scale: GPUs depreciate quickly, resale is messy, and the rack space, power, and cooling are recurring commitments. Worse, buying now would let our allocation dysfunction persist and grow. If we double the fleet while utilisation stays at 40%, we have doubled our capital tied up in idle silicon and learned nothing. There is also an opportunity cost: the same budget could fund a scheduling and observability layer, engineering time to right-size workloads, and a reserve for the moment when we genuinely do need to buy — at which point we would buy with real data rather than frustration.

**What improving utilisation actually buys us**

The utilisation path is slower and requires discipline, but it is cheap, reversible, and diagnostic. A simple job queue with time limits and preemption, better batch sizing, quantised models where full precision is unnecessary, and honest instrumentation of who is using what would likely lift effective utilisation substantially. Just as valuable, it would produce the evidence we need: if, after two months of proper scheduling, queues are still long and cards are genuinely saturated, then the case for purchase becomes airtight and we will know exactly what to buy. If utilisation jumps and the queues vanish, we have saved a large capital outlay and learned that our problem was process, not capacity.

**Reliability and latency, honestly weighed**

I want to be fair to the other side here. Scheduling layers add friction: a queue means waiting, and preemption means some jobs get interrupted. There is a real risk that a poorly implemented scheduler makes life worse before it makes it better, and a team under deadline pressure may reasonably experience a queue as a regression even when aggregate throughput improves. Reliability also has a human dimension — shared hardware with enforced limits means people plan ahead rather than grabbing resources ad hoc, which is a behavioural change we cannot mandate into existence overnight. These are genuine risks, and they are the strongest argument for the purchase path.

**Recommendation**

I recommend we commit to a two-month utilisation improvement effort before any purchase decision: deploy a shared scheduler with time limits, instrument utilisation properly, and audit our largest workloads for waste. We should set an explicit trigger — if p95 queue wait for a standard job exceeds a defined threshold after the improvement window, we proceed to procurement with the team's full support. This keeps the option to buy open, avoids spending capital to paper over an allocation problem, and ensures that if we do buy, we buy once and buy right.

I acknowledge real uncertainty here: our utilisation data is imperfect, and it is possible the fleet is genuinely saturated in ways the averages hide. That is precisely why the first step is better measurement. If the data surprises us, we adapt. I'd like a decision by end of week so we can start the scheduling work immediately.

Questions and dissent welcome — this is a decision we should make together.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Status: Recommendation to defer hardware purchase; invest one quarter in utilisation work**

We've reached the point where our inference workloads are bumping against capacity during peak hours, and the obvious question on the table is whether we buy more GPUs or squeeze more out of the fleet we already own. I want to make the case that we should treat this as a utilisation problem first and a procurement problem second, and to be honest about where that reasoning could be wrong.

The financial argument is the easiest to state. Our current fleet is running at roughly 40% average utilisation, with peaks above 85% and overnight troughs near 10%. That gap between average and peak is the whole story. Buying hardware to cover peak demand means paying for capacity that sits idle most of the day, and at current prices a modest expansion would consume most of our remaining hardware budget for the year. Before we commit that money, we owe ourselves a serious attempt to flatten the peaks and fill the troughs. If we can lift average utilisation to 60% through better batching, smarter scheduling, and moving batch workloads into off-peak windows, we effectively buy the equivalent of half a fleet expansion for the cost of a few engineering weeks.

Latency is the counterweight, and I don't want to minimise it. Some of our utilisation inefficiency exists because we've deliberately left headroom: we queue conservatively, we batch less aggressively than we could, and we keep models resident in memory that could be swapped. Every one of those choices was made for a reason, and unwinding them risks p95 latency regressions that our product teams will feel immediately. This is why the utilisation work needs to be treated as real engineering with real guardrails, not a quick win. We should set explicit latency SLOs before touching scheduler configuration, and treat any regression beyond agreed thresholds as a stop signal. If we find that the latency-sensitive paths genuinely cannot absorb more packing, that itself is valuable information — it tells us the headroom we see on dashboards is not actually harvestable, and it strengthens the case for hardware.

Reliability cuts both ways. A denser, more heavily utilised fleet has less slack to absorb failures. Today, when a node goes down, we shed load onto idle capacity and users barely notice. At 70% utilisation, the same failure becomes a visible incident. But this argues for better capacity management, not necessarily more metal: if we improve our ability to drain, reschedule, and degrade gracefully, we can be both denser and more resilient than we are now. Buying hardware without fixing our failure-handling would just mean we fail more expensively.

The opportunity cost question deserves plain language. Every dollar spent on GPUs this year is a dollar not spent on the evaluation pipeline, the fine-tuning work, and the two product integrations currently competing for the same budget. Hardware is also the least reversible line item we have. GPUs depreciate, they lock us into a rack footprint and a power contract, and if our workload mix shifts — say, toward smaller models or toward a hosted API for low-stakes traffic — we cannot easily un-buy them. Utilisation work, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible. If we spend six weeks on scheduling and batching and it doesn't move the needle, we've lost some engineering time and learned something specific about our constraints. That asymmetry matters more than the headline price of either option.

So my recommendation is concrete: we defer the purchase decision by one quarter, spend that time on measured utilisation improvements with latency SLOs as the guardrail, and re-evaluate with real numbers in hand. If utilisation reaches 60% or better and peak pressure is manageable, we likely defer purchase indefinitely. If we hit hard latency or reliability walls, we will have a much sharper procurement case — and possibly a smaller one, since partial gains still reduce what we need to buy.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Utilisation projects have a way of expanding, and there's a real risk we spend the quarter optimising and still end up buying hardware, having delayed relief for the teams feeling the squeeze now. If peak-hour contention is already causing dropped work or missed commitments, we should say so and consider a small, targeted purchase alongside the utilisation work rather than treating this as strictly either/or. My read is that our current pain is scheduling pain, not capacity pain, but I hold that view with maybe 70% confidence, and the quarter's data should settle it.

Happy to walk through the utilisation numbers and the proposed SLOs with anyone before we decide.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Status and problem**

Our inference cluster is running hot. Peak-hour utilization on our eight A100s has crept above 85 percent, queue times during business hours have tripled since the spring, and we've had two incidents in the last month where batch jobs were preempted to keep interactive latency within SLO. The obvious question on the table is whether to buy four more cards. I've spent the last two weeks looking at the utilization data, our cost structure, and what the alternatives actually cost us, and I want to lay out a recommendation before we commit capital.

**The case for buying**

The straightforward argument for purchase is that our utilization is already high, which by conventional wisdom means we're capacity-constrained and should add hardware. There's truth in that. But high utilization is not the same as efficient utilization. When I broke down the workload mix, roughly a third of our GPU-hours are going to batch fine-tuning and evaluation runs scheduled with no regard to the interactive traffic curve. Another meaningful slice is lost to model-loading overhead, because services cold-start their weights on every job rather than keeping warm replicas. In other words, a substantial fraction of our "capacity problem" is a scheduling and lifecycle problem wearing a capacity costume.

**The case for improving utilization first**

The financial picture reinforces this. Four A100s at current pricing, plus the networking, chassis, and power provisioning to run them properly, is a seven-figure commitment with a three-to-four-year depreciation horizon. That capital is not free: the same money would fund two additional engineers for a year, or a serious investment in our evaluation pipeline, both of which we've deprioritized for lack of budget. And the commitment is only partially reversible. GPUs hold resale value reasonably well, but the rack space, power contracts, and operational attention do not unwind cleanly. If our workload mix shifts — say, if we migrate the batch pipeline to a hosted training service, or if model distillation lets us serve most traffic on smaller accelerators — we'd be carrying stranded capacity.

Latency is the strongest argument on the buy side, and I want to be honest about it. Scheduling improvements can smooth average utilization, but they cannot conjure headroom at the 99th percentile. If a traffic spike coincides with a batch window, our interactive p99 will suffer no matter how clever the scheduler is. That said, our latency SLO breaches are concentrated in two predictable windows tied to our own batch schedule, not to organic traffic. Moving batch jobs to overnight and capping their concurrency is a configuration change, not a research project.

**Reliability**

There's also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More cards means more redundancy, which is real: right now a single node failure removes a quarter of our capacity. But our two recent incidents were both caused by contention and preemption, not hardware failure. Better isolation — separate queues, memory limits, and a dedicated small pool for latency-sensitive traffic — addresses the failure mode we actually have. Hardware redundancy addresses one we've been lucky to avoid. I'd rather fix the failure mode we've observed and revisit redundancy when we have evidence we need it.

**Recommendation**

I recommend we defer the purchase for one quarter and instead fund a focused utilization effort: reschedule batch workloads off peak hours, implement warm model serving for our top three services, and put proper queue isolation between interactive and batch traffic. My estimate, based on the workload breakdown, is that these changes free 25 to 35 percent of effective capacity — roughly the equivalent of two to three new cards — at a fraction of the cost. We should pre-approve the purchase decision for the end of the quarter with a clear trigger: if measured p99 latency or queue depth still breaches targets after the scheduling work lands, we buy, and we buy with the confidence that the remaining constraint is genuine rather than self-inflicted.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag the honest limits of this analysis. My utilization numbers come from sampling rather than continuous tracing, so the batch share could be off by several points in either direction. Warm serving is well-understood for our model sizes but adds memory pressure we haven't fully modeled. And if the business wins a large new customer in the next quarter, all of this arithmetic changes and we should buy immediately. The point of the recommendation is not that hardware is bad; it's that we should spend a quarter making sure we're buying capacity rather than buying a fix for our own scheduling. Sequencing the cheap, reversible work first costs us weeks. Sequencing it wrong costs us seven figures.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** Buy more GPU hardware, or get more out of what we already own?
**Date:** Thursday

**Summary and recommendation**

We have been asked whether we should purchase additional local AI hardware or invest in improving the utilisation of the machines we already run. After looking at our cost structure, latency profile, reliability history, and the opportunity cost of each path, my recommendation is that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing fleet, and defer any purchase decision until we have real evidence that the constraint is capacity rather than scheduling. I want to be clear that this is a recommendation made under genuine uncertainty, not a certainty dressed up as one, and I'll explain where the uncertainty lives.

**The cost picture**

The purchase option is expensive in ways that are easy to see and in ways that are easy to forget. The visible cost is the capital outlay itself, which at current prices would consume most of our hardware budget for the year. The less visible costs are power, cooling, rack space, and the engineering time to integrate and operate new machines. There is also depreciation to consider: accelerator hardware has historically lost resale value quickly as new generations arrive, so a purchase made today is a bet that we will extract value faster than the market erodes it.

Utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly an investment of our own time. Batching improvements, better queueing, model quantisation, and smarter placement of workloads across our existing cards cost us engineering hours rather than cash. Those hours are not free, but they are hours we would spend anyway on operational firefighting if we keep running hot. The marginal cost of a percentage point of utilisation is far lower than the marginal cost of a percentage point of new capacity.

**Latency**

Latency is the strongest argument for buying more hardware. If our interactive workloads are queueing behind batch jobs, users feel it, and no amount of clever scheduling fully removes that pain when the fleet is genuinely saturated. But our telemetry suggests we are not saturated. Peak-hour utilisation sits in a range that leaves real headroom, and our p99 latency spikes correlate with batch jobs landing on top of interactive traffic rather than with raw capacity limits. If that diagnosis is right, better isolation and scheduling could recover most of the latency we've lost without buying anything. If the diagnosis is wrong, we will find out quickly during the utilisation quarter, and we can revisit the purchase with better data.

**Reliability**

Reliability cuts both ways. More machines mean more redundancy, so a single card failure is less likely to take down a service. But more machines also mean more components that can fail, more drivers to keep in sync, and a larger surface for the kind of silent degradation that has bitten us twice this year. Improving utilisation raises the stakes on each existing machine: when we run closer to capacity, a failure hurts more. That is a real cost of the utilisation path, and it argues for pairing any utilisation push with modest investment in failover and graceful degradation, which we need regardless of which direction we choose.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The deepest question is what we give up. Money spent on hardware this year is money not spent on hiring, oning, or on the product work that actually differentiates us. Time spent on utilisation is time not spent shipping features. On the hardware side, the commitment is largely irreversible: once purchased, accelerators are hard to redeploy and harder to sell without loss. Utilisation work is the opposite — it is highly reversible. If we improve our scheduling and batching and then discover we still need capacity, nothing is wasted; those improvements make any future fleet cheaper and more effective. If we buy first and discover we didn't need to, the money is gone.

**Where I could be wrong**

I want to flag the honest uncertainties. Our utilisation numbers come from coarse instrumentation, and it is possible that the true bottleneck is memory bandwidth or interconnect rather than compute, in which case scheduling improvements will disappoint. Our workload mix may also shift — if a new product line lands, demand could double in a quarter and make this whole analysis moot. That is why I'm proposing a bounded utilisation effort with an explicit checkpoint, not an open-ended refusal to buy.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next quarter on utilisation, with a defined review at the end. If utilisation gains plateau below what demand requires, buy then, with evidence in hand. The reversible option first, the irreversible one only when it's proven necessary.

Happy to discuss at Monday's sync.

**Internal Memo — Infrastructure Team**

**Re: Buy more GPUs, or use the ones we have better?**

**From:** Engineering Lead, ML Platform
**To:** Engineering team, Finance partner

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the easy answer is to buy more hardware, and I want to make sure we don't take that path without thinking it through. Our GPU cluster is running hot — queue times for training jobs have crept up, our inference fleet sits at high utilization during peak hours, and several people have asked, reasonably, when we're ordering more cards. The question on the table is whether we should expand our local fleet or invest the same money in getting more out of what we already own. My recommendation, which I'll defend below, is that we spend the next quarter on utilization before we spend a single dollar on new silicon.

Let's start with cost, because it's the least ambiguous part of this decision. The quotes we've gathered for expanding the fleet land in the range of what our entire annual engineering budget foring and platform work would be, once you include networking, power, cooling, and the rack space itself. And that's just the capital cost. Hardware depreciates, power bills are recurring, and every card we buy is a commitment we'll be servicing for years whether or not our workload justifies it. By contrast, the utilization work — better job scheduling, batch-size tuning, quantization for inference, killing the zombie notebooks that quietly reserve GPUs nobody uses — costs engineer time, which is real but far cheaper and, crucially, it's time that builds durable skill in the team. When I audited our own dashboards last week, I found that our headline utilization number of 78 percent is flattering: measured against actual demand rather than reservations, the true figure is closer to 50 percent. That gap is, in effect, a fleet we already own and aren't using.

Latency is the argument for buying, and I take it seriously. Interactive work — fine-tuning experiments, prototype inference, the debugging loop our researchers live in — suffers when jobs queue behind batch workloads. Slow feedback loops have a real cost in engineering productivity, and it doesn't show up on any invoice. But this is precisely the kind of problem that utilization work solves better than expansion does. A scheduler that preempts low-priority batch jobs, a separate queue for interactive work, and honest accounting of who is holding what will do more for perceived latency than doubling capacity while letting the same bad habits scale up with it. Buying hardware without fixing scheduling is like adding lanes to a road with no traffic lights: congestion returns, and now we've paid for it twice.

Reliability cuts the other way, and here I want to be honest about the tradeoff. A larger fleet gives us redundancy. If a node fails today, we feel it; if we had twice the nodes, we'd feel it less. There's also a case that running everything near saturation shortens hardware life and makes failures more frequent and more visible. I don't want to dismiss this. But our reliability posture is currently weak in ways that more hardware won't fix — we lack good failure telemetry, our checkpointing is inconsistent, and recovery is manual. Those are utilization-and-operations problems, and solving them makes the fleet we have more trustworthy, which matters more to our users than theoretical redundancy we can't orchestrate.

Then there's opportunity cost and reversibility, which I think are the decisive framing. Money spent on hardware is spent; the cards will hold some resale value, but the market for used accelerators is volatile and we'd be selling into whatever the cycle looks like in two years. Money spent on utilization work is largely recoverable in the sense that it produces knowledge,ing, and processes that carry forward regardless of what hardware we eventually own. And the reverse is true too: if we buy now and our workload shifts — if a hosted API becomes good enough for part of our inference load, or a project gets deprioritized — we're stuck with sunk capital and a fixed cost base. Utilization improvements keep our options open. They also give us better data: after a quarter of honest measurement and scheduling work, we'll know our real demand curve, and if expansion is still justified, we'll buy the right amount instead of guessing.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My utilization numbers come from our own instrumentation, which we all know has gaps, and it's possible that a serious audit reveals our demand is genuinely higher than I believe. It's also possible that the scheduling work proves harder than estimated — scheduler projects have a way of growing — and that we end up six months from now needing hardware anyway, having spent time instead of getting ahead of the problem. If demand growth is as steep as some forecasts suggest, deferring purchase only delays the inevitable. These are real risks, and I don't think we can eliminate them;
